title: HTTP connection churn and decoding tail-latency: multi-sku benchmark notes
summary: Working notes for an experiment that measures how short-lived HTTP connection patterns (high churn) interact with token decoding latency across multiple GPU SKUs and driver/CUDA combos. Focus is on p95/p99 decode tail amplification when requests are numerous and small, and on how TLS/keep-alive and frontend termination choices mitigate or amplify effects.
content:
Objective:
This doc captures exploratory experiments to quantify how HTTP connection churn (lots of short-lived requests, small payloads) amplifies token-decode tail latency across different cloud GPU SKUs (A100 / H100 / L40S) and driver + CUDA combinations. We want to simulate realistic customer traffic patterns (many small chat turns over HTTP) and identify mitigations (keep-alive, connection pooling, TLS termination placement, per-node accept queue sizing, tokenization on edge).

Motivation and hypothesis:
- Observed customer symptom: sporadic p99 decode spikes (~2-5x baseline) for chat workloads where the frontend opens many short connections per turn (or customers disable keep-alive).
- Hypotheses:
  1) Short-lived connections cause CPU spikes at the edge (TLS handshakes, accept() syscall churn) that preempt inference worker threads and increase kernel-launch jitter on GPUs, amplifying decode p95/p99.
  2) Different GPU SKUs show different sensitivity because of driver-level polling/interrupt handling and NVLink/PCIe DMA concurrency characteristics.
  3) Driver + CUDA versions change kernel launch latency and CPU-side preparation timing leading to SKU-differentiated tail behavior.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Cloud SKUs tested: AWS p4d.24xlarge (A100), AWS p5.48xlarge (H100), GCP L40s-equivalent instance (L40S).
- Models: 13B open model (prefill+stream decode), sequence length 64 prompt + decode up to 128 tokens.
- Runtime: Redwood serving runtime (local lab branch w/ debug telemetry), latest internal container consistent across SKUs.
- Driver / CUDA pairs:
  - Driver 525 + CUDA 11.7 (baseline)
  - Driver 535 + CUDA 11.8
  - Driver 545 + CUDA 12.1
- Frontend patterns:
  - Keep-alive ON (persistent connections, 50 connections per loadgen thread)
  - Keep-alive OFF (fresh connection per HTTP request)
  - TLS termination at LB (ELB/NLB) vs node-local TLS (nginx sidecar)
  - Tokenization: client-side vs server-side tokenization (tokenization cost adds CPU work in server-side case)
- Load patterns: baseline QPS 200 (low concurrency), spike QPS 1800 (many concurrent tiny requests), synthetic Poisson arrival to simulate burstiness.

Key measurements: p50/p95/p99 decode latency (end-to-end), CPU rps on inference node, kernel-launch latencies (via runtime tracing), accept-rate and TLS handshake time, context-switch rates.

Selected results (representative, numbers are median of 3 runs):
- Baseline (Keep-alive ON, LB TLS):
  - p50/p95/p99 (A100, driver525): 46ms / 72ms / 108ms
  - p50/p95/p99 (H100, driver525): 42ms / 70ms / 112ms
  - p50/p95/p99 (L40S, driver525): 58ms / 96ms / 160ms
- High churn (Keep-alive OFF, node-local TLS, server-side tokenization) at spike QPS:
  - A100 (525/11.7): 62ms / 148ms / 412ms  (p99 amplification ~3.8x)
  - H100 (525/11.7): 55ms / 134ms / 386ms  (p99 amplification ~3.4x)
  - L40S (525/11.7): 78ms / 210ms / 690ms  (p99 amplification ~4.3x)
- Driver/CUDA upgrade effect (Keep-alive OFF case above, same load):
  - A100 (545/12.1): 60ms / 128ms / 310ms  (p99 drops ~25% vs 525)
  - H100 (545/12.1): 50ms / 116ms / 290ms  (p99 drops ~25%)
  - L40S (545/12.1): 74ms / 190ms / 540ms  (still worst but improved)
- TLS termination placement: node-local TLS increased CPU syscall load by ~12-18% and moved some latency off LB -> slightly worse p95/p99 by ~5–10% in churned scenarios compared to LB termination.
- Keep-alive ON (persistent) dramatically reduces p99 amplification: e.g., A100 (525) p99 drops from 412ms to 126ms under same QPS when long-lived connections are used.

Observations / interpretation:
1) Connection churn is a first-order amplifier of decode tail latencies. The major noisy component is CPU-side work (TLS, accept, tokenization) that can preempt or contend with threads handling GPU work, leading to kernel-launch jitter and longer queues for KV cache population.
2) L40S showed relatively higher sensitivity in these experiments. Possible causes: driver thread affinity/interrupt handling differences, or memory/fabric throughput characteristics that amplify when CPU-side jitter exists. L40S improved with driver/CUDA upgrades but remains more sensitive at p99.
3) Newer driver/ CUDA versions (545/12.1) reduced kernel launch and CPU->GPU prep overheads across the board, trimming p99 significantly. However, software-level mitigations (keep-alive, LB TLS) produce the largest effect.
4) Node-local TLS can be useful for certain compliance paths, but it increases per-node CPU pressure and can worsen tail latency under churn. Offloading TLS to LB (or using hardware TLS) is better for tail control in high-churn patterns.
5) Client-side tokenization is a low-effort mitigation: moving tokenization out of the inference node removed a common CPU spike and reduced p99 by ~20–30% in churned tests.

Actionable mitigations tested / recommended:
- Default to keep-alive (persistent) connections for chat-turn style workloads. Provide SDK guidance and quickstart that enables sane connection pooling.
- Encourage client-side tokenization by default; provide reference tokenization libs in SDKs.
- Prefer LB-level TLS termination where compliance allows; if node-local TLS required, size accept queues and increase process concurrency on edge proxies to avoid CPU head-of-line blocking.
- Upgrade driver/CUDA across fleet to the tested 545/12.1 stack (or whatever upstream vendors recommend) after regression testing — gives measurable p99 improvements even under churn.
- For L40S-heavy fleets, add additional tail-specific guardrails: smaller per-model concurrency limits, proactive autoscale thresholds, and stronger CPU reservation for network/TLS threads.
- Instrument runtime to surface kernel-launch jitter and to correlate TLS/accept spikes with GPU-side telemetry. Existing traces need a join key between socket events and request ids.

Open follow-ups and experiments:
- Repeat with mixed-tenant noisy neighbors on same host (we only tested single-tenant but with heavy CPU work). Hypothesis: multi-tenant noise will further amplify p99 on L40S.
- Test with very long context lengths (2k+) to see interaction of KV-cache repopulation with connection churn.
- Measure effect of keep-alive timeouts and max-connections-per-IP in frontends; find operational sweet spots for shared infra.
- Try offloading tokenization to a lightweight sidecar that shares CPU budget but is scheduled with priority to avoid stealing cycles from GPU workers.

Experiment notes / commands (how we ran it):
- Loadgen: custom harness based on wrk2 + small python harness to orchestrate tokenization modes. Scripts in github: repo/inference-benchmarks/benchmarks/http-churn/*
- Runtime tracing: enabled experimental trace flags: REDWOOD_TRACE=timestamps,kernel-launch,accept; aggregated in internal trace UI.
- Driver install notes: used vendor AMIs and driver packages installed via apt; validated nvidia-smi and nvprof output.

Quick checklist for follow-up rollout plan (eng-serving-runtime):
- [ ] Add connection-pool guidance to SDK quickstarts and sample apps (docs + code).
- [ ] Add a telemetry join key from socket accept -> request id in runtime (priority).
- [ ] Schedule driver/CUDA upgrade pilot in staging fleet with A/B traffic and synthetic churn.
- [ ] Add a canned benchmark in release-tests that runs churned small-request workload and asserts p99 < 350ms for 13B model on A100 baseline.

Notes/confounds:
- These runs were done in lab accounts with different OEM AMIs; cloud hypervisor noise varies by region. Absolute numbers are not production SLAs but the relative deltas between keep-alive vs churn and driver versions are robust across runs.
- We did not test custom kernel parameter tuning (tcp_tw_reuse, accept4 flags) which might help at OS level.

Appendix: quick raw table (representative single-run numbers)
SKU | Driver/CUDA | Keepalive | TLS | p95 | p99
A100 | 525/11.7 | ON | LB | 72ms | 108ms
A100 | 525/11.7 | OFF | node-local | 148ms | 412ms
A100 | 545/12.1 | OFF | node-local | 128ms | 310ms
H100 | 525/11.7 | OFF | node-local | 134ms | 386ms
H100 | 545/12.1 | OFF | node-local | 116ms | 290ms
L40S | 525/11.7 | OFF | node-local | 210ms | 690ms
L40S | 545/12.1 | OFF | node-local | 190ms | 540ms
